For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

The test-function topology exists as a Hausdorff locally convex vector topology, induces the prescribed topology on each $\mathcal D_K$, and is the finest locally convex topology making all inclusions $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous. A linear map $L:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to E$ to a locally convex space is continuous if and only if each restriction $L|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous. An increasing compact exhaustion whose interiors cover $\Omega$ gives the same topology, independently of the exhaustion. Thus this is an LF topology of the complete metrizable fixed-support spaces. All these claims hold in ZF.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be the state domain of a conservation system, $n\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $|n|=1$, and $s\in\mathbb R$. The planar interface and its two open sides are
$$\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st=0\},\qquad Q^-=\{n\cdot x-st<0\},\qquad Q^+=\{n\cdot x-st>0\}.$$
A state field is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$ if on each side it is $C^1$ and, near every point of $\Sigma$, each side field is the restriction of a $C^1$ map from a neighborhood in $I\times\Omega$ into $\mathcal O$. The left and right traces $U_L,U_R:\Sigma\to\mathcal O$ are the restrictions of those extensions to $\Sigma$; they are independent of the chosen extensions because they agree with the same field on their respective open sides. For any state or flux quantity $G$ with these traces, define its jump by $[G]=G_R-G_L$. A planar shock profile is such a piecewise $C^1$ state field with its specified constant interface normal $n$ and speed $s$; the definition does not assert that it solves a conservation system.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The integral identity is required only when the displayed integrands are locally integrable on the test support.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data, add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ and require $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. A weak solution satisfying this inequality is entropy-admissible relative to that pair.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix a test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$. In a local orthogonal spatial chart write $x=y+(st+r)n$, with $y\in n^\perp$ and $r=n\cdot x-st$. The resulting affine coordinate map $(t,y,r)\mapsto(t,x)$ has absolute determinant $1$; [F4] therefore gives the volume change and [F5] permits iterated integration of the compactly supported integrands. Let $H(r)=1$ for $r>0$ and $H(r)=0$ for $r<0$. By [F3], one-dimensional integration by parts in $r$ gives, for every $C^1$ coefficient field $a$, $\partial_t(aH)=H\partial_ta-s\,a|_\Sigma\delta_\Sigma$ and $\partial_{x_j}(aH)=H\partial_{x_j}a+n_j\,a|_\Sigma\delta_\Sigma$, where $\delta_\Sigma$ pairs with $dt\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}_x$ on the spatial plane. The time derivative is at fixed $x$, so in this chart $\partial_t|_x=\partial_t|_{y,r}-s\partial_r$; this produces the factor $-s$ and the stated normalization. Tangential spatial derivatives have no boundary term, while the normal derivative contributes $n_j$.

On a neighborhood of $\Sigma$, write $U=U_L+[U]H$ and $F_j(U)=F_j(U_L)+[F_j(U)]H$, using the $C^1$ side extensions from [F1]. Apply the derivative formulas of step 1.1. The regular terms are the classical residuals on the two open sides, hence vanish by the given equations; the remaining interface term is $\left(\sum_jn_j[F_j(U)]-s[U]\right)\delta_\Sigma$. A partition of unity over the compact support of $\varphi$ gives the same formula throughout $I\times\Omega$.

If the coefficient vanishes on $\Sigma$, the residual distribution is zero. Conversely, if it is nonzero at a point of $\Sigma$, continuity of the traces gives a neighborhood on which one component has a fixed strict sign. A nonnegative compactly supported test in that interface patch, placed in the corresponding vector component, has a nonzero pairing with the residual, contradicting that it is the zero distribution. If $\Sigma$ is empty in the cylinder, the equivalence is vacuous. Thus the residual vanishes exactly when the vector Rankine–Hugoniot equality holds pointwise on $\Sigma$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The integral identity is required only when the displayed integrands are locally integrable on the test support.

$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. $$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$

$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$

By [F2], the chain rule and compatibility give, pointwise for each $\epsilon>0$,
$$\partial_t\eta(u^\epsilon)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j(u^\epsilon)=\epsilon\eta'(u^\epsilon)\Delta u^\epsilon.$$
Applying the chain rule twice in each spatial coordinate and the product rule yields $\eta'(u^\epsilon)\Delta u^\epsilon=\Delta\eta(u^\epsilon)-\eta''(u^\epsilon)|\nabla u^\epsilon|^2$. Since $\eta''\geq0$, the entropy residual is at most $\epsilon\Delta\eta(u^\epsilon)$.

Multiply by $\psi\geq0$ and integrate. By [F4], the integrals can be taken iteratively in time and each spatial coordinate. Applying [F3] to the smooth compactly supported products gives integration by parts twice in each spatial coordinate and once in time, with $\psi$ vanishing near $T$, and yields
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\eta(u^\epsilon)\psi_t+\sum_jq_j(u^\epsilon)\psi_{x_j}\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\eta(u_0^\epsilon)\psi(0,x)\,dx\geq-\epsilon\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\eta(u^\epsilon)\Delta\psi\,dx\,dt.$$
These integrations by parts are the one-dimensional FTC applied to the smooth compactly supported products in each coordinate and in time; no spatial boundary term remains.

The functions $\eta$ and $q_j$ are Lipschitz and bounded on $[-M,M]$. Thus [A2] implies local $L^1$ convergence of $\eta(u^\epsilon)$ and $q_j(u^\epsilon)$ to $\eta(u)$ and $q_j(u)$, and of $\eta(u_0^\epsilon)$ to $\eta(u_0)$. Moreover, the absolute value of the right-hand side in step 2.1 is at most $\epsilon\sup_{[-M,M]}|\eta|\int|\Delta\psi|$, which tends to zero. Passing to the limit yields the stated entropy inequality.

   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(H_{u,c}) = 0$, and so is every subset of it.
2. Every proper linear subspace $W \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ a hyperplane is the singleton $\{c/u_0\}$ and the only proper linear
subspace is $\{0\}$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be the state domain of a conservation system, $n\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $|n|=1$, and $s\in\mathbb R$. The planar interface and its two open sides are
$$\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st=0\},\qquad Q^-=\{n\cdot x-st<0\},\qquad Q^+=\{n\cdot x-st>0\}.$$
A state field is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$ if on each side it is $C^1$ and, near every point of $\Sigma$, each side field is the restriction of a $C^1$ map from a neighborhood in $I\times\Omega$ into $\mathcal O$. The left and right traces $U_L,U_R:\Sigma\to\mathcal O$ are the restrictions of those extensions to $\Sigma$; they are independent of the chosen extensions because they agree with the same field on their respective open sides. For any state or flux quantity $G$ with these traces, define its jump by $[G]=G_R-G_L$. A planar shock profile is such a piecewise $C^1$ state field with its specified constant interface normal $n$ and speed $s$; the definition does not assert that it solves a conservation system.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The integral identity is required only when the displayed integrands are locally integrable on the test support.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data, add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ and require $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. A weak solution satisfying this inequality is entropy-admissible relative to that pair.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
